szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence Aids Pediatric Bronchiolitis Diagnosis but Demands Rigorous Clinical Validation

A comprehensive narrative review published in Frontiers in Medicine evaluates the developing role of artificial intelligence in the computer-assisted diagnosis and differential diagnosis of pediatric bronchiolitis. Bronchiolitis is one of the most common acute lower respiratory tract illnesses affecting infants and young children, predominantly occurring in children under two years of age with the highest incidence during infancy. Across international healthcare systems, the disease represents a major cause of pediatric emergency visits and hospital admissions. The diagnosis of bronchiolitis remains primarily clinical, relying on detailed medical histories and physical examinations. Established medical guidelines indicate that routine chest imaging, blood tests, and virological investigations are generally unnecessary in typical presentations. However, hallmark symptoms including cough, tachypnea, wheezing, crackles, and increased work of breathing overlap extensively with pneumonia, viral-induced wheezing, and early childhood asthma. These clinical similarities create persistent diagnostic hurdles, particularly in young infants and early stages of illness.

Authored by Tianyang Lan and Fuyao Zhang alongside corresponding author Zhenqi Wu from Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, the study surveyed scientific literature indexed across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through September 2026. The authors observed that artificial intelligence models do not redefine existing diagnostic criteria but convert subjective auditory, imaging, and clinical features into quantifiable parameters. To clarify the evidentiary landscape, the review established a three-tiered classification framework. Level I represents relatively strong direct evidence, encompassing studies that specifically evaluated bronchiolitis using patient-level, multicenter, or external validation cohorts. Level II denotes preliminary direct evidence addressing bronchiolitis through smaller single-center datasets, internal validation, or severity prediction. Level III covers indirect supportive evidence derived from investigations into pneumonia, asthma, pathogen detection, or abnormal acoustic classification. Across all categories, the authors excluded preprints and unreviewed manuscripts, focusing solely on formally published academic investigations, reviews, and clinical guidelines.

Digital respiratory sounds and cough acoustics currently represent the data sources most directly linked to automated bronchiolitis diagnosis. A landmark prospective multicenter pediatric study conducted by Porter and colleagues provided Level I evidence by combining automated cough acoustic analysis with routine clinical variables. Their system achieved successful patient-level classification across common pediatric conditions, differentiating bronchiolitis from pneumonia and asthma. In contrast, research by Bisballe-Müller and collaborators demonstrated that traditional perceptual features assessed by clinicians, such as classifying coughs as dry or wet and calculating cough frequency, could not reliably distinguish bronchiolitis from asthma or pneumonia. This finding indicates that simple audible characteristics lack sufficient diagnostic resolution, underscoring the necessity for deep computational models capable of extracting complex spectral patterns and temporal dynamics. By analyzing high-dimensional acoustic signatures, machine-learning systems can identify subtle acoustic variations that human ears cannot consistently detect, offering objective support for difficult differential assessments.

Large-scale auscultation research has demonstrated further diagnostic progress through international cohorts. The DeepBreath study, led by Heitmann and colleagues, evaluated automated respiratory-sound models using digital lung auscultation recordings collected from 572 children across five separate nations. DeepBreath achieved robust patient-level classification of bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and wheezing disorders while maintaining accuracy across international cohorts, delivering critical Level I validation for acoustic artificial intelligence. Concurrently, technical investigations have focused on automated identification of adventitious sounds such as crackles and wheezes. TaghiBeyglou and colleagues introduced TRespNET, which mapped time-frequency representations into convolutional neural networks to classify abnormal pediatric respiratory audio. In parallel, Kim and collaborators applied a Transformer-based deep-learning architecture to pediatric wheeze detection, utilizing model explainability techniques to localize the specific time-frequency acoustic regions driving classification decisions.

However, implementing acoustic artificial intelligence in routine pediatric healthcare faces substantial hardware, environmental, and behavioral barriers. In real-world hospital environments, such as Hoekstra and colleagues’ evaluation of digital auscultation among children with pneumonia in Malawi, automated sound analysis proved feasible at bedside. Yet Pais-Cunha and colleagues discovered that when consumer smartphones recorded pediatric lung sounds, algorithmic performance declined markedly due to surrounding room noise, low recording quality, and patient age. Furthermore, Park and colleagues reported substantial disparities in machine-learning accuracy across different categories of abnormal pediatric respiratory sounds, confirming that isolated sound detection does not equal reliable disease classification. The review authors stress that future acoustic development must transition from basic detection of isolated wheezes or crackles toward modeling complete respiratory cycles, cough sequences, and multidimensional acoustic phenotypes validated across noisy emergency rooms and outpatient pediatric clinics.

Medical imaging provides valuable diagnostic insight in select clinical scenarios, although routine radiography is not recommended in standard bronchiolitis management. Consequently, the primary utility of chest radiograph artificial intelligence lies in identifying alternative diagnoses like pneumonia rather than establishing bronchiolitis directly. Chen and colleagues proved that deep-learning networks can automatically recognize radiographic features of pediatric pneumonia. Similarly, Yazdani and colleagues deployed explainable prototype networks to detect pneumonia on pediatric radiographs, localizing explanatory image patches. Li and collaborators demonstrated that anatomical region segmentation refined pneumonia identification and radiographic lesion localization. Nevertheless, cross-domain generalizability remains problematic. Agarwal and colleagues transferred commercial artificial intelligence systems developed for adult radiographs to pediatric cohorts, revealing sharp drops in diagnostic performance influenced by patient age and lesion type. Furthermore, Togunwa and colleagues reported severe performance degradation when models trained on public datasets were tested in geographically independent populations, confirming that radiographic models require rigorous pediatric-specific validation before clinical deployment.

Lung ultrasonography represents an appealing diagnostic modality for infants and young children because it eliminates ionizing radiation and allows convenient bedside re-evaluation. Magrelli and colleagues applied convolutional neural networks to lung ultrasound images, performing three-class classification among healthy infants, children with bronchiolitis, and patients with bacterial pneumonia. Their deep-learning model identified machine-recognizable features including B-lines, pleural line irregularities, and pulmonary consolidations, offering preliminary Level II direct evidence.
